stem: Which enzyme breaks down the neurotransmitter at a cholinergic synapse?

options.content: Acetylcholinesterase
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: ATP synthase
options.rationale: ATP synthase makes ATP in mitochondria.

options.content: Choline kinase
options.rationale: Not the enzyme that hydrolyses acetylcholine in the cleft.

options.content: Monoamine oxidase
options.rationale: This acts on other transmitters such as noradrenaline, not on acetylcholine.

explanation: **Acetylcholinesterase** hydrolyses acetylcholine into choline and ethanoic acid.

stem: Which ions enter the presynaptic knob when an action potential arrives, triggering the release of acetylcholine?

options.content: Calcium ions
options.rationale: Correct: through voltage-gated calcium channels.

options.content: Sodium ions
options.rationale: Na⁺ enters the postsynaptic cell when ACh binds.

options.content: Potassium ions
options.rationale: K⁺ leaves during repolarisation.

options.content: Chloride ions
options.rationale: Chloride is not the trigger for exocytosis.

explanation: Voltage-gated **calcium** channels open; Ca²⁺ entry causes vesicles to fuse with the membrane.

stem: By which process is acetylcholine released from the presynaptic membrane?

options.content: Facilitated diffusion
options.rationale: ACh is released in vesicles, not through channels.

options.content: Active transport by a carrier
options.rationale: Release is by vesicle fusion, not by a carrier protein.

options.content: Osmosis
options.rationale: Osmosis is the movement of water.

options.content: Exocytosis
options.rationale: Correct: vesicles fuse with the membrane.

explanation: Vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release ACh by **exocytosis**.

stem: Why can impulses cross a synapse in one direction only?

options.content: The synaptic cleft is far too wide for any ions to diffuse across it in the reverse direction
options.rationale: Neither ions nor impulses cross the cleft in either direction.

options.content: Only the presynaptic side releases transmitter; only the postsynaptic side has receptors
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: Acetylcholinesterase is found only on the presynaptic membrane
options.rationale: The enzyme is on the postsynaptic side; this is not the reason.

options.content: The postsynaptic membrane is always in its refractory period
options.rationale: It is not permanently refractory.

explanation: Vesicles are only presynaptic and receptors only postsynaptic, so transmission is one-way.

stem: An organophosphate insecticide inhibits acetylcholinesterase. What happens at a cholinergic synapse after poisoning?

options.content: No ACh is released, so no impulses cross
options.rationale: Release is not affected; breakdown is.

options.content: ACh receptors are blocked, so sodium channels cannot open
options.rationale: That describes a receptor blocker such as curare.

options.content: ACh stays bound, so the postsynaptic membrane stays depolarised
options.rationale: Correct: continuous stimulation.

options.content: Calcium channels stay closed in the presynaptic knob
options.rationale: The insecticide acts on the enzyme in the cleft.

explanation: ACh is not hydrolysed, so it keeps binding and the sodium channels keep opening: continuous stimulation, spasm and possible respiratory failure.
hints: What does the enzyme normally do?

stem: Nicotine stimulates some cholinergic synapses. The best explanation is that nicotine

options.content: inhibits acetylcholinesterase so that ACh gradually accumulates in the synaptic cleft
options.rationale: That is the action of organophosphates.

options.content: has a shape similar to ACh and binds to its receptors, opening the channels
options.rationale: Correct: it mimics ACh.

options.content: enters the presynaptic knob and is packaged into synaptic vesicles
options.rationale: Nicotine acts on postsynaptic receptors.

options.content: opens voltage-gated calcium channels in the postsynaptic membrane
options.rationale: Ca²⁺ channels involved in release are presynaptic.

explanation: Nicotine is similar enough in shape to ACh to bind some ACh receptors and open their sodium channels.

stem: Impulses arrive at the same moment at three synapses on one postsynaptic neurone. None alone reaches threshold, but together they produce an action potential. This is

options.content: temporal summation
options.rationale: Temporal summation is repeated impulses in one neurone.

options.content: saltatory conduction
options.rationale: That is conduction along a myelinated axon.

options.content: synaptic fatigue
options.rationale: Fatigue is running out of transmitter.

options.content: spatial summation
options.rationale: Correct: inputs from several neurones add together.

explanation: Several presynaptic neurones together: **spatial** summation.
hints: Several neurones, or one neurone firing repeatedly?

stem: Many mitochondria are found in the presynaptic knob. Which is the best explanation?

options.content: ATP is needed for ACh to diffuse across the synaptic cleft
options.rationale: Diffusion is passive.

options.content: Mitochondria release calcium ions that trigger exocytosis
options.rationale: The Ca²⁺ that triggers release enters from the tissue fluid.

options.content: ATP is needed to open the voltage-gated sodium channels
options.rationale: Voltage-gated channels open in response to depolarisation, not ATP.

options.content: ATP is needed to resynthesise ACh and to pump Ca²⁺ out of the knob
options.rationale: Correct.

explanation: ATP is used to make ACh from choline and acetate (via acetyl coenzyme A), to move vesicles and to pump Ca²⁺ out.

stem: Acetylcholine enters the postsynaptic neurone and causes depolarisation.
explanation: False. ACh binds to receptors on the surface; the receptor channels open and **sodium ions** enter.

stem: The products of acetylcholine hydrolysis are taken back into the presynaptic knob and used to make more acetylcholine.
explanation: True. Choline and ethanoic acid diffuse back and ACh is resynthesised, using ATP.

stem: Match each structure of a cholinergic synapse with its function.

right.content: Binds ACh and opens a sodium channel
Lets calcium ions into the knob

explanation: Vesicles store; Ca²⁺ channels admit Ca²⁺; receptors bind ACh; the enzyme removes it.

stem: Choose the correct words.

payload.template: Acetylcholine diffuses across the synaptic {{blank:a}} and binds to receptors on the {{blank:b}} membrane, causing {{blank:c}} ions to enter.

explanation: Cleft → postsynaptic receptors → sodium ions in.

stem: Name the two products of the hydrolysis of acetylcholine.
explanation: **Choline** and **ethanoic acid** (acetate).

stem: A pathway contains 4 synapses, each with a delay of 0.6 ms. The axons in the pathway have a total length of 1.1 m and conduct at 55 m s⁻¹. Calculate the percentage of the total transmission time that is due to synaptic delay. Give your answer to three significant figures.
explanation:
1. Conduction time $= \dfrac{1.1}{55} = 0.02\ \text{s} = 20\ \text{ms}$.
2. Synaptic delay $= 4 \times 0.6 = 2.4\ \text{ms}$.
3. Total $= 20 + 2.4 = 22.4\ \text{ms}$.
4. Percentage $= \dfrac{2.4}{22.4} \times 100 = 10.7\%$.
Dividing by the conduction time only (12.0%) is a common mistake.
workedSolution:
1. Conduction time $= \dfrac{1.1}{55} = 0.02\ \text{s} = 20\ \text{ms}$.
2. Synaptic delay $= 4 \times 0.6 = 2.4\ \text{ms}$.
3. Total $= 20 + 2.4 = 22.4\ \text{ms}$.
4. Percentage $= \dfrac{2.4}{22.4} \times 100 = 10.7\%$.
Dividing by the conduction time only (12.0%) is a common mistake.
hints: Find the conduction time first, in ms.
Divide the synaptic delay by the TOTAL time.

stem: A postsynaptic membrane has a resting potential of -68 mV and a threshold of -52 mV. Each impulse arriving at the synapse depolarises it by 5 mV, and the effects add if impulses arrive close together. What is the smallest number of impulses in rapid succession needed to produce an action potential?
explanation: Depolarisation needed = -52 − (-68) = 16 mV. 16 ÷ 5 = 3.2, so **4** impulses are needed (3 give only 15 mV). This is temporal summation.
workedSolution: 1. Depolarisation needed = -52 − (-68) = 16 mV. 16 ÷ 5 = 3.2, so **4** impulses are needed (3 give only 15 mV). This is temporal summation.
hints: Work out how many mV are needed to reach threshold.

stem: Describe the sequence of events at a cholinergic synapse from the arrival of an action potential to the production of an action potential in the postsynaptic neurone.

points.description: Action potential arrives at the presynaptic knob and opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels
Ca²⁺ diffuses into the knob
Vesicles move to and fuse with the presynaptic membrane, releasing ACh by exocytosis
ACh diffuses across the synaptic cleft
ACh binds to (complementary) receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, opening Na⁺ channels
Na⁺ diffuses in, depolarising the postsynaptic membrane; if threshold is reached an action potential is produced

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The action potential depolarises the presynaptic knob and opens voltage-gated calcium channels, so calcium ions diffuse in. This causes vesicles of acetylcholine to move to the presynaptic membrane and fuse with it, releasing ACh into the cleft by exocytosis. ACh diffuses across the cleft and binds to complementary receptor proteins on the postsynaptic membrane, opening their sodium channels. Sodium ions diffuse in and depolarise the postsynaptic membrane; if the threshold is reached, an action potential is generated.

explanation: Six steps in order.

stem: Explain why it is important that acetylcholine is broken down rapidly after it has bound to receptors.

points.description: So that sodium channels close and the postsynaptic membrane repolarises
Prevents continuous stimulation / repeated action potentials from one impulse
Allows separate impulses to be transmitted / the products are recycled to make more ACh

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Hydrolysis of ACh lets the receptor channels close so the postsynaptic membrane repolarises. Without it, the postsynaptic cell would be stimulated continuously by one impulse. Rapid removal allows each new impulse to be transmitted separately, and the products are recycled to make more ACh.

explanation: Stop the signal, allow the next one.
hints: What would happen if ACh stayed bound?

stem: Suggest why farm workers spraying organophosphate insecticides are advised to wear gloves, masks and protective clothing.

points.description: Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase in humans as well as in insects
They can be absorbed through the skin or lungs
ACh accumulates, causing continuous stimulation of muscles: twitching, spasm, breathing difficulty / possible death

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase in humans as well as insects, because the enzyme is similar. They can be absorbed through the skin and lungs. Acetylcholine would then build up at synapses and neuromuscular junctions, causing continuous stimulation, muscle twitching and spasm, and possibly failure of breathing.

explanation: Same enzyme, same effect.
hints: Does the human nervous system use the same enzyme?

stem:
A drug Z was added at different concentrations to the fluid bathing a cholinergic synapse. The same stimulus was applied each time, and the size of the depolarisation of the postsynaptic membrane was recorded as a percentage of the value with no drug.

| Concentration of Z / µmol dm⁻³ | 0 | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 | 10 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Postsynaptic depolarisation / % | 100 | 82 | 61 | 45 | 30 | 18 |

The amount of acetylcholine released did not change with the concentration of Z.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage decrease in the postsynaptic depolarisation when the concentration of Z increased from 0 to 6 µmol dm⁻³.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Describe the effect of Z on the postsynaptic depolarisation.

points.description: As concentration increases, the depolarisation decreases
Quoted data: from 100% at 0 to 18% at 10 µmol dm⁻³ / falls steadily without levelling off

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: As the concentration of Z increases, the postsynaptic depolarisation decreases, from 100% with no drug to 18% at 10 µmol dm⁻³, falling steadily across the whole range.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Which mode of action of Z best fits these results?

options.content: Z inhibits acetylcholinesterase
options.rationale: This would increase or prolong depolarisation.

options.content: Z blocks voltage-gated calcium channels in the knob
options.rationale: ACh release would then fall, but it did not.

options.content: Z binds to ACh receptors without opening their channels
options.rationale: Correct: ACh release is unchanged but its effect falls.

options.content: Z mimics ACh and opens sodium channels
options.rationale: A mimic would increase depolarisation.

parts.explanation: Release is unchanged, so Z must act on the postsynaptic side; reduced depolarisation means fewer receptor channels open: Z blocks receptors.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why Z at high concentration would prevent an action potential in the postsynaptic neurone.

points.description: Z occupies many receptors, so ACh cannot bind
Fewer Na⁺ channels open, so less Na⁺ enters
Depolarisation does not reach the threshold, so no action potential

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: At high concentration Z occupies most of the receptor sites, so acetylcholine cannot bind to them. Fewer sodium channels open and less Na⁺ enters, so the depolarisation of the postsynaptic membrane is too small to reach the threshold and no action potential is generated.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Suggest one way of checking that the reduced response was not caused by fatigue of the synapse.

points.description: Wash out Z and stimulate again (response returns to 100%) / allow rest between stimuli / test the concentrations in random order

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Wash Z out and repeat the stimulus: if the response returns to 100%, fatigue was not the cause.

explanation: Unchanged release with reduced response points to a receptor blocker.
hints: Is Z acting before or after the cleft?

stem: An electron micrograph of a synapse shows a swollen axon ending containing many small round vesicles and several mitochondria, a narrow gap, and a dark thickened region on the membrane of the cell opposite.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Name the neurotransmitter stored in the vesicles at a cholinergic synapse.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Suggest what the dark thickened region on the opposite membrane contains, and why it is needed.

points.description: Many receptor proteins / ligand-gated sodium channels (and acetylcholinesterase)
To bind ACh so that Na⁺ channels open / to depolarise the postsynaptic membrane

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: It contains a high density of receptor proteins (ligand-gated sodium channels), which bind acetylcholine and open so that the postsynaptic membrane is depolarised.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain the role of the mitochondria in the axon ending.

points.description: Aerobic respiration supplies ATP
For resynthesis of ACh / packaging into vesicles / pumping Ca²⁺ out

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Mitochondria supply ATP by aerobic respiration, which is used to resynthesise acetylcholine from choline and acetate, to fill vesicles and to pump calcium ions out of the knob.

explanation: Presynaptic vesicles and mitochondria, cleft, postsynaptic receptors.
hints: Work from the presynaptic side across.
